title: Trees more often have separate sexes than other plants

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Trees more often have separate sexes than other plants

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Trees, across all plant orders, have separate male and female flowers more often than other plants do, which helps pollen move between trees (though Hooker reported the rule fails in Australia).

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: That trees belonging to all Orders have their sexes more often separated than other plants, I find to be the case in this country

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter IV, “Natural Selection”; section “On the generality of intercrosses between individuals of the same species”. Scope: flowering plants, comparing trees with non-woody plants

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch04-13: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.80

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Both variables are standard categorical traits and broad public compilations exist. Harmonization is manageable and a contemporary comparative test can directly confirm or refute the stated association.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Code growth form and sexual system across flowering plants and compare the frequency of dioecy or separate flowers in trees versus non-woody plants using phylogenetic regression. A robust positive tree effect supports the claim; no effect or a negative effect refutes it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Sexual-system coverage is incomplete and terminology varies.

Regional sampling could obscure a global pattern.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Sexual system and growth form are standard coded variables, and the confirming result is a phylogenetically repeated excess of separate sexes in trees. Global flora and sexual-system databases cover enough orders and regions, including the Australian case Darwin already flagged, for that test. A small team can run the comparative model in weeks; residual gaps would change the estimate, not the design of the test.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Join sexual system to woody versus non-woody growth form and fit a phylogenetic model, including a regional term for Australia. A higher probability of separate sexes in trees, repeated across orders, would confirm the association; no difference, or a difference confined to one or two clades, would refute it as a general rule.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Tropical trees are less completely coded than temperate floras.

Growth-form and sexual-system definitions differ among sources and must be harmonized.

Separate sexes and woodiness both cluster phylogenetically, so an uncorrected count would mislead.

fields.label: Hypothesis
fields.value: Among flowering plants, species that are trees have separate sexes (dioecy or monoecy, i.e. unisexual flowers) more often than non-woody (herbaceous) species, and this excess recurs across orders rather than being confined to one or two clades.

fields.label: Method
fields.value: GIFT trait 3.4.1 (sexual system; 2,977 species) was joined to trait 1.2.1 (growth form; 222,598 species, 23 API pages) by work_ID, species were assigned to orders and to Angiospermae through the GIFT nested-set taxonomy, and 1,865 angiosperm species with a single growth-form value (146 trees, 242 shrubs, 1,477 herbs) were analysed. Separate sexes (dioecious or monoecious) in trees vs herbs was tested with a Fisher exact test (odds ratio), with trees vs shrubs and dioecy-only as supplementary comparisons, and the direction of the difference checked within each order having >= 10 trees and >= 10 herbs.

fields.label: Pass criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered. Using the GIFT database public API, join the sexual-system trait (3.4.1: dioecious / monoecious / bisexual) to the growth-form trait (1.2.1: tree / shrub / herb / other) for angiosperm species (Angiospermae in the GIFT taxonomy), keeping species whose growth-form value is a single category. 'Separate sexes' = dioecious or monoecious. The claim is SUPPORTED if (i) the odds ratio of separate sexes in trees versus herbs is >= 1.5 with two-sided Fisher exact p < 0.01, and (ii) among orders with at least 10 trees and at least 10 herbs in the joined data, the proportion of species with separate sexes is higher in trees than in herbs in at least two-thirds of orders.

fields.label: Fail criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered. The claim is REFUTED if the odds ratio is <= 1.0 or p >= 0.05, or if trees exceed herbs in fewer than half of the qualifying orders. Other outcomes are 'mixed'. Supplementary: the same odds ratio for trees vs shrubs, for dioecy alone, and the proportion of separate-sexed species in each growth form.

fields.label: Unit
fields.value: odds ratio of separate sexes (dioecious or monoecious) in trees versus herbs, angiosperms in GIFT

fields.label: Interpretation
fields.value: Darwin's 'trees' is read as GIFT growth form 'tree'; 'other plants' primarily as herbs (the claim's scope says 'comparing trees with non-woody plants'), with shrubs reported separately; 'sexes separated' as dioecious or monoecious (both have unisexual flowers, which is what Darwin's argument about cross-pollination needs); 'belonging to all Orders' as the across-order replication test. Darwin's observation was for Britain ('in this country') with Hooker's report of failure in Australia; the GIFT data are global, so the test is of the generalisation rather than the British observation. Modern caveat known in advance: GIFT sexual-system coverage (~3,000 species) is a small, non-random subset of angiosperms, so coverage bias is possible in either direction.

fields.label: Datasets
fields.value:
GIFT (Global Inventory of Floras and Traits) public API: traits 3.4.1 (Reproduction sexual) and 1.2.1 (Growth form), species list

GIFT public API: taxonomy (nested set of genera, families, orders, Angiospermae)

fields.label: Caveats
fields.value:
GIFT sexual-system coverage is small (2,977 species, 1,865 usable angiosperms) and evidently enriched for dioecious species (55% of the trees and 7% of the herbs are dioecious, against roughly 6% of all angiosperms), so absolute proportions are not representative; the test relies on the contrast between growth forms, which would be biased only if the references coding sexual systems targeted dioecious trees more than dioecious herbs. Published syntheses with larger samples (e.g. Renner 2014; Vamosi et al. 2003) report the same association of dioecy with woody growth.

Only three orders (Apiales, Malpighiales, Rosales; derived/orders.csv) have >= 10 trees and >= 10 herbs with sexual-system data; trees exceed herbs in all three, but a sign test on three orders cannot be significant (p = 0.125), so the 'across all Orders' part of the claim is only weakly tested.

Shrubs are intermediate (60% separate-sexed), and trees still exceed shrubs (OR 2.1, p = 0.001), so the effect is not just woody vs herbaceous.

Species are treated as independent; no phylogenetic correction was applied, and the growth-form categories ignore within-species variation (species with mixed growth-form values were excluded).

Hooker's reported failure of the rule in Australia was not tested separately, since GIFT trait values are not regionalised.
